newsitem.title: ITALY: ALPINE SKIING-TOMBA GOES OUT AS THE QUIET MAN WINS.
newsitem.headline: ALPINE SKIING-TOMBA GOES OUT AS THE QUIET MAN WINS.

text.p: Switzerland's Michael Von Gruenigen, the antithesis of Alberto Tomba, won the men's giant slalom at the Alpine skiing world championships on Wednesday and took away the Italian showman's crown.
Tomba's long-awaited first race at the championships lasted for barely one minute and ended when the giant and slalom world champion pulled up on the first run.

Von Gruenigen, a quiet family man who shuns the media spotlight, seized his first world title with an elegant and commanding performance from start to finish to take Switzerland's second gold in Sestriere.
The World Cup giant slalom champion's winning time was two minutes 48.23 seconds, 1.12 ahead of Norway's Lasse Kjus who picked up his third silver medal.

Andreas Schifferer of Austria was the surprise bronze medallist, starting 17th in the first leg and then moving up from ninth place at the start of the second to beat Switzerland's Steve Locher by just 0.03 of a second.

A surprise qualifier in the Austrian team, his podium place came only a year after he suffered severe bruising of the brain in a downhill training crash in Kitzbuehel. Strangely, Kjus also suffered concussion in a fall in the same session.
Tomba's fans had been gathering near the piste in the north-western Italian resort since daybreak and were out in force with their banners and klaxons to cheer on the home hero.

But they fell silent when the 30-year-old triple Olympic gold medallist nearly fell. Tomba, realising it was a useless endeavour to try to get back into the race, called it a day and skied off the piste.
Various Italian dignitaries, including local Olympic committee head Mario Pescante and world athletics boss Primo Nebiolo, left soon after in disappointment.
While Tomba "La Bomba" was left with time on his hands and headed off for lunch, Von Gruenigen used the interval between the two legs to play with his three-year-old son.
The Swiss man, whose fans have so far come up with no more imaginative nickname than MVG, said he had learned a lot from defeat by Tomba at the Sierra Nevada championships last year.

He said Tomba had not been a worry for him, given the Italian's poor form in giant this season, and he had been more concerned about Kjus and Norway's combined gold medallist Kjetil-Andre Aamodt who was fourth after the first run.

"Last year I was the favourite for the event but I could not deal with the pressure," said Von Gruenigen, who is the first Swiss since the great all-rounder Pirmin Zurbriggen won in Crans Montana in 1987 to capture a giant world title.
"I learned a lot from last year and found I could put the pressure on the others," he said. "This was my biggest goal this season and I feel I deserved this medal."

Von Gruenigen, who has won two World Cup giants this season, was the first out of the start house on the first run and took advantage of the clean snow to clock by far the fastest time. Later starters found it far harder to keep to the line.
Six of the first 15 starters crashed out, including some of the pre-race favourites such as Swiss Urs Kaelin.
Tomba complained that the run had been too long and the conditions, with patches of light and shade, treacherous. Others also said how much they disliked the first leg.
"I'm very sorry. But Saturday will be my day," Tomba said, referring to the closing men's slalom.

Austrian Toni Sailer, who won three golds at the 1956 Olympics, defended the layout of the first run and said it was the sort of traditional and highly demanding giant slalom that had gone out of fashion in recent years.
Kjus, who also won silver in the downhill and super-G, had no complaints about his race.
"The championships are over for me now and I'm going home to enjoy my medals," the 1996 World Cup overall champion said after his first medal in the technical discipline.
The race had the biggest line-up of the championships so far, with 110 entrants.
